<!-- Generated by tools/refgen. Edit the source it names, not this file. -->

The file an installation starts from - `installation_config` in Terraform. It seeds the control plane's database once; after that the dashboard edits the installation, and a later change to the file shows up there as a proposal to apply or dismiss. Every block is optional. Check a file before applying it with `controlplane config check <file>`.

```yaml title="spin.yaml"
# An installation's configuration, as a file to keep in git.
#
#   controlplane config check spin.yaml   # what it declares; opens no database
#
# The file seeds an installation: when a control plane starts, each item here the installation
# does not have yet is created from it, once. From then on the installation is its database, and
# the dashboard edits all of it. A later file that says something else of an item - a changed
# default, a policy taken out - is not written: the dashboard shows it as a change to apply or
# dismiss, and remembers the answer until the file changes again.
#
# Every block is optional.

settings:
  # What a workspace may be created from. Declared and empty is refused: it would allow
  # nothing at all. Leave the key out for the installation's default.
  allowed_images:
    - ghcr.io/acme/sandbox:v1
  # Whether a workspace has to belong to a team.
  require_team_for_workspace: false
  # Zero is no limit.
  max_workspaces_per_user: 10
  # Whether the object store's garbage collection, a daily job, only says what nothing reaches
  # rather than deleting it. The delete is a marker the bucket expires after its Object Lock.
  storage_gc_report_only: false
  # What a workspace created without a tag of its own runs under, by policy name - the
  # network_policies block below, or a host's own. Unset, it is "offline", the policy every
  # host has and which allows nothing: a workspace nobody chose a policy for reaches nothing
  # past its own namespace. An agent creating its own workspaces is exactly the caller that
  # names no tag, so this is where an installation decides what that one may reach.
  #
  # Declared empty it is "offline" as well: no spelling of this setting means open. An
  # installation that wants such a workspace to reach the internet declares a policy that says
  # so - allow: ["0.0.0.0/0"], which the node's own drops still come before - and names it
  # here, so what a workspace may reach always has a name somebody chose.
  default_network_tags:
    - agent
  # Moving a workspace off a host that stopped answering, without anybody asking.
  #
  # A host that *stops* says so and is emptied first. This is the other one: the machine that
  # lost power, or its network, and said nothing. Its workspaces stay where they are until
  # somebody runs `spin workspace recover --accept-data-loss`, which means noticing.
  #
  # rehome_after_seconds is how long the silence has to last; unset or zero, nothing is ever
  # moved and this whole thing is off, which is what an installation starts as. A move gives
  # up whatever the host had not published, so it is not a default.
  #
  # rehome_max_unpublished_bytes is how much of that this installation gives up on its own.
  # The number is what the silent host last reported it had not sent to the object store -
  # for a host that is gone, what it never will. Over it, the workspace waits for a person.
  # A host that never reported at all also waits: nothing known is not the same as nothing
  # to lose.
  rehome_after_seconds: 900
  rehome_max_unpublished_bytes: 67108864
  # Where this installation keeps its logs and traces: a bucket of its own, never the volumes',
  # in the same account and region as theirs. The control plane that leads runs the store over
  # it; a change of bucket is applied by restarting it. How many days each index keeps what it
  # holds is read again every minute; 30, 7 and 7 where a key is left out.
  logs_bucket: acme-spin-logs
  logs_platform_retention_days: 30
  logs_workspace_retention_days: 7
  traces_retention_days: 7
  # Keep what every workspace writes - its machine's console, and what its own services write to
  # the guest's journal - searchable by whoever may read the workspace for
  # logs_workspace_retention_days. Off unless declared: that output leaves its workspace only
  # when the installation decides it does. Each workspace may have logs_workspace_daily_mb of it
  # kept a UTC day (100 where this says nothing); past it, the rest of the day is dropped and one
  # line says so.
  collect_workspace_logs: false
  logs_workspace_daily_mb: 100

registration:
  # open, whitelist or closed.
  mode: whitelist
  # Addresses and domains the whitelist admits. An entry with an @ is an address; without
  # one, a domain.
  emails:
    - acme.com
    - contractor@example.com

# What a person may choose when creating a workspace. One preset may be the default.
presets:
  - name: small
    description: For an agent doing one task at a time
    cpu: 2
    memory_mb: 4096
    disk_gb: 20
    default: true
  - name: large
    cpu: 8
    memory_mb: 16384
    disk_gb: 100

# Egress policies, by name. A workspace created with --network-tag agent runs under this one.
#
# Carrying a tag is the deny. A workspace with no tag reaches anything beyond the node's own
# networks; a workspace with any tag reaches what its tags allow and nothing else. So every
# policy here is an allowlist.
#
# "offline" is not declared here and cannot be: every host installs it, it allows nothing, and
# it is what default_network_tags means when it is unset.
#
# Tags compose as a union: a workspace created with two of them reaches everything either one
# allows, and the order they are named in does not change that.
#
# allow is IPv4 prefixes; allowNames are names, each exact or with a single leading "*.",
# enforced through the workspace's own lookups - the host opens the address its resolver
# answered that workspace with, for as long as the answer lives. allowPorts are destination
# ports at any address, "443" being TCP, which is what a bare number means; UDP is asked for
# by name ("53/udp"), because opening UDP to anywhere is the shape of a tunnel, and "icmp" is a
# ping - an echo request, no other ICMP type. A workspace needs no port for DNS: its resolver
# is the host's, which answers under every policy.
#
# A policy is as exact as DNS: an address serving several names is open to all of them once
# one is allowed. See docs/network/README.md.
network_policies:
  - name: agent
    allowNames:
      - github.com
      - "*.githubusercontent.com"
      - registry.npmjs.org
    allow:
      - 140.82.112.0/20
  # The web and nothing else: no address at all, so it composes with any other tag.
  - name: web
    allowPorts:
      - 80
      - 443
```
